title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Solid pseudopapillary epithelial neoplasms (SPENs) of the pancreas are rare tumors now recognized as low-grade malignant neoplasms with low metastatic potential and excellent survival rates. These tumors predominantly affect young women, though cases occur in males and across pediatric and older adult populations. In adults, lesions more commonly arise in the pancreatic body or tail, while pediatric cases often involve the pancreatic head. This course reviews the clinical presentation of SPENs, which often has a prolonged asymptomatic course, frequently delaying diagnosis until tumors reach large sizes or are incidentally detected on imaging. Additionally, when patients do present with symptoms, they are typically nonspecific and result from compression of adjacent structures.

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity explores SPEN epidemiology, pathogenesis, imaging characteristics, diagnostic strategies, and treatment options. Participants should expect to enhance their ability to recognize SPENs, interpret relevant imaging and pathology findings, as advances in imaging, pathology, and molecular understanding have improved diagnostic accuracy and management. Evidence-based management approaches, postoperative complications, and follow-up considerations to improve patient outcomes are also discussed. This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to enhance the learner's competence in identifying SPENs, performing the recommended evaluation, and implementing an appropriate interprofessional approach when managing this condition.

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Introduction
content: Solid pseudopapillary epithelial neoplasms (SPEN) of the pancreas are rare pancreatic tumors first described by Dr. Virginia Kneeland Frantz in 1959. These neoplasms were previously known by various names, including solid and cystic tumors of the pancreas, Frantz tumors, solid and papillary epithelial neoplasms, Hamoudi tumors, and papillary-cystic tumors. Though SPENs were considered benign for a significant amount of time, these tumors have now been reclassified as low-grade malignant tumors with low metastasis rates and high survival rates. [1] They typically occur in young women, though these neoplasms can occasionally be seen in males and in pediatric and older populations. In adults, they occur more frequently in the body or tail of the pancreas, while in children, they are most often seen in the pancreatic head. [2]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Introduction
content: Patients are usually asymptomatic for prolonged periods, and by the time symptoms have developed, tumors have typically grown to considerably larger sizes. Less frequently, SPENs may invade adjacent structures or metastasize to distant organs. An accurate and prompt diagnosis is paramount in minimizing complication rates and improving patient outcomes.

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Etiology
content: The etiology of SPENs remains unclear, but the hypothesis with the most convincing evidence thus far is that SPENs originate from the pluripotent cells of the genital ridges that adhere to the pancreas during early embryogenesis. Features supporting this theory include the sex and age distribution, the absence of pancreatic markers, and the expression of sex hormone receptors. Some SPENs tend to regress after menopause, further supporting this hypothesis. [2]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Etiology
content: An overwhelming majority of SPENs carry mutations in CTNNB1 , which is the gene encoding ß-catenin, thus resulting in its nuclear accumulation. [3] A rare association between SPEN and familial adenomatous polyposis has also been documented in existing literature. Inactivation of the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene and subsequent activation of the Wnt/ß-catenin pathway likely explain this association. [4]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Epidemiology
content: Solid pseudopapillary epithelial neoplasms account for 1% to 2% of exocrine pancreatic lesions and approximately 5% of cystic pancreatic lesions in adults. [2] [5] In pediatric populations, these tumors comprise between 6% and 17% of all pancreatic neoplasms. [2] Recent literature describes a 7-fold increase in incidence over the past 2 decades. While this trend may represent a true rise in case frequency, multiple authors attribute the increase to advances in imaging modalities and improved diagnostic techniques. [6]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Epidemiology
content: A marked female predominance characterizes these neoplasms, with a reported female-to-male ratio of 10:1. The age at detection ranges from 8 to 67 years, with an average age of 28.5 years at diagnosis. [7] In male patients, diagnosis typically occurs earlier, with a reported mean age of 18.5 years. [8]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Histopathology
content: On gross examination, solid pseudopapillary epithelial neoplasms appear large and well encapsulated, with a variegated cut surface that includes foci of necrosis, hemorrhage, and cystic change. Vascular ischemia has been proposed as the primary explanation for this heterogeneous appearance. [9] Microscopic evaluation demonstrates marked regional variation in cellular architecture. The solid components consist of sheets or cords of homogeneous cells interspersed with numerous blood vessels. Widespread areas of cystic degeneration are common, and pseudopapillary formations with pseudorosettes are pathognomonic features of these neoplasms. Detachment of tumor cells from supporting blood vessels leads to the development of the pseudopapillary pattern. Cercariform cells represent a consistent cytologic finding and serve as a key distinguishing feature from pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. [2] Mitotic activity remains uncommon.

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Histopathology
content: Features suggesting malignant transformation include exophytic growth pattern, incomplete encapsulation, calcifications, invasion of pancreatic parenchyma or neurovascular structures, and metastases. [10] Immunohistochemical analysis typically demonstrates positivity for ß-catenin, the dot-like pattern of CD99, vimentin, neuron-specific enolase, alpha-1-antitrypsin, and alpha-1-antichymotrypsin. Identification of CTNNB1 mutations alone often suffices for diagnostic confirmation. [2] [6] These neoplasms do not demonstrate elevated tumor markers, eg, cancer antigen 19-9 or carcinoembryonic antigen. [11]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- History and Physical
content: SPENs typically have a long asymptomatic period before developing any signs or symptoms. Most often, due to the indolent nature of these tumors, they are incidentally diagnosed on physical examination or upon obtaining imaging studies for other medical reasons. When patients are symptomatic, their symptoms result from the SPEN compressing adjacent organs.

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- History and Physical
content: Symptoms, when present, are nonspecific and include abdominal pain or discomfort, diarrhea, or nausea. Rarely, jaundice or gastric outlet obstruction may develop depending on the location of the SPEN. To date, no endocrine functional imbalances have been associated with these tumors. [6] As previously mentioned, SPENs have low malignant potential. In cases of malignant transformation, the liver is the most common site of metastasis. Other metastasis sites include regional lymph nodes, the mesentery or omentum, and the peritoneum. [8]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: Although SPENs may be incidentally detected on physical exam, clinical diagnosis is impossible due to various differentials. The tumor has a distinctive morphology on imaging and is usually located in the body or tail of the pancreas. On computer tomography (CT) imaging, SPENs are characteristically thick-walled, encapsulated structures with peripheral solid and central cystic components. Furthermore, an important differentiating feature of SPENs from other pancreatic neoplasms is that SPENs enhance similarly to the surrounding pancreatic parenchyma with contrast. [12]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Evaluation -- Imaging Studies
content: However, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is considered superior to CT in the diagnosis of SPENs. On MRI, SPENs appear heterogeneous, with varying signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. [5] The capsule appears as a thin hypointense rim. Additionally, angiographies may further help delineate SPENs from surrounding tissues, which may be necessary for determining tumor resectability.

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Evaluation -- Pathology Studies
content: A preoperative pathological diagnosis is best obtained via endoscopic ultrasound-guided biopsy and remains the diagnostic gold standard. [13] Different regions of this heterogeneous tumor have been found to have varying pathological and immunohistochemical patterns; therefore, biopsies must be taken from several sites to ensure an accurate diagnosis. [14]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Treatment / Management
content: Surgical parenchyma-preserving enucleation frequently provides curative treatment and represents the preferred therapeutic approach for solid pseudopapillary epithelial neoplasms. In select cases, tumors are considered unresectable because of invasion or encasement of major surrounding arteries, including the aorta, superior mesenteric artery, or celiac artery. Under such circumstances, alternative therapeutic modalities warrant consideration, including radiofrequency ablation, gamma-knife treatment, arterial embolization, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy. [15]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Treatment / Management
content: Approximately 75% of these tumors express estrogen and progesterone receptors, supporting a potential role for systemic tamoxifen therapy when surgical resection cannot be pursued. [16] Evidence supporting tamoxifen use remains limited, as no clinical trials have evaluated this approach, and reported success derives solely from isolated case reports.

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The clinical presentation at the time of diagnosis is variable and could resemble other pathologic entities; therefore, the definitive diagnosis relies on radiological findings and immunohistological assessments. Differential diagnoses that should also be considered when evaluating SPENs include: Mucinous cystic neoplasms of the pancreas Islet cell tumors Neuroendocrine tumors with cystic features (eg, cystadenoma or cystadenocarcinoma) Serous microcystic adenoma Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN)

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Medical Oncology
content: Unresectable, metastatic, and recurrent cases of SPEN may require radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or hormonal therapy. Studies on these treatment modalities are limited, and further research is needed to develop management guidelines. Nevertheless, evidence suggests that SPENs are radiosensitive and respond favorably to systemic chemotherapy and hormonal therapy. [5] Specifically, chemotherapeutic regimens with floxuridine and oxaliplatin, etoposide and cisplatin, or S-1 have proven successful. [15]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Staging
content: At present, no specific pathological staging systems exist for SPENs. However, these tumors can be staged based on the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) TNM staging system for high-grade or malignant tumors. [17]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Prognosis
content: The overall prognosis of SPENs remains relatively favorable due to minimal aggressiveness. However, these tumors tend to be more aggressive when they occur in older males. [7] Approximately 10% to 15% of all SPENs show highly malignant behavior and metastasize. Though tumor size, lymphovascular invasion, and the Ki-67 index have been proposed as predictors of aggressiveness and relapse, evidence is scant, and further research is needed. [18] The overall 5-year survival rate is about 97%. [19]

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Complications
content: Most complications are associated with compression of adjacent structures, resulting in jaundice and gastric outlet obstruction. In the postoperative period, complications include pancreatic fistulas, pancreatitis, steatorrhea, infections, bleeding, biliary fistulas, and ileus. Additionally, the development of diabetes mellitus is seen in less than 1% of patients. [20] Although rare, close follow-up is recommended to monitor for recurrence or metastasis.

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Deterrence and patient education play a central role in improving outcomes for patients with SPENs of the pancreas, given the absence of established screening strategies for early detection. These tumors often follow a prolonged asymptomatic course and frequently reach large sizes before diagnosis, increasing the risk of local compression, complications, or delayed intervention. Patient education focused on symptom recognition remains essential, particularly awareness of persistent or unexplained abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, early satiety, or abdominal fullness. Early recognition and referral are important, as timely surgical resection is highly effective and often curative, underscoring the value of symptom-based vigilance and early engagement with healthcare services. Educating patients to seek prompt medical evaluation for such persistent or unexplained symptoms supports earlier imaging, diagnosis, and referral, which may reduce morbidity associated with advanced tumor growth.

title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Key facts to keep in mind regarding SPENs include: SPENs are uncommon and often indolent pancreatic tumors. SPENs are commonly present in young women, suggestive of the possible role of hormonal factors. Diagnosis of these tumors is by diagnostic imaging and biopsy. The definitive treatment is surgery, often curative in most cases and associated with excellent long-term prognosis. These neoplasms should be considered in the differential diagnosis of cystic pancreatic tumors, specifically in a young woman. Despite the indolent nature of SPENs, most patients require surgical resection. Surgery can be curative regardless of the tumor's size or location, and local recurrence or metastasis after complete resection is rare. In unresectable or metastatic cases, systemic therapies are often necessary, though formal treatment guidelines are lacking.

content: SPENs of the pancreas represent rare, low-grade malignant tumors that predominantly affect young women and often follow a prolonged asymptomatic course. Diagnosis frequently occurs incidentally or after tumors reach considerable size, emphasizing the importance of clinical vigilance and imaging expertise. title: Solid Pseudopapillary Epithelial Neoplasm (SPEN) of the Pancreas -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimal management requires coordinated interprofessional collaboration focused on patient-centered care. Physicians, general practitioners, and advanced practitioners rely on strong assessment skills to recognize concerning symptoms, initiate appropriate imaging, and expedite referrals. Radiologists and histopathologists contribute specialized expertise to confirm diagnosis, while surgeons and oncologists collaborate on individualized treatment planning. Nurses support patient education, perioperative monitoring, and follow-up adherence, while pharmacists assist with medication management and adverse effect monitoring when nonsurgical therapies are required. Effective interprofessional communication and care coordination enhance patient safety, streamline transitions across care settings, and improve outcomes through timely intervention and comprehensive follow-up.
